title: Quotations, Reporting Clauses and Indirect Questions
summary: Report statements and thoughts in your own words or with accurate quotations; position reporting clauses naturally; distinguish negatives in the reporting and reported clauses; and construct embedded wh- and yes/no questions with statement word order.
learningObjectives: Distinguish direct quotations from reports containing a reporting clause and a reported clause.
Place reporting clauses around quotations and use natural subject–verb order, especially with pronoun subjects.
Choose the appropriate position of a negative depending on whether the speaker did not report something or reported a negative fact.
Form reported wh-questions and yes/no questions with wh-, if- or whether-clauses and non-inverted word order.

explanation.heading: Report the meaning or quote the actual words
explanation.body: A report in the writer’s own words normally combines a reporting clause (the speaker and reporting verb) with a reported clause expressing the message. The reported clause may begin with that, a wh-word, if or whether, depending on its grammatical role. Direct quotation reproduces the speaker’s exact words and uses quotation marks; reporting indirectly may adjust person, time references and tense to fit the new viewpoint.
explanation.example: Direct: “I need an extra day,” Noor said. Indirect: Noor said that she needed an extra day.

explanation.heading: Where reporting clauses go with quotations
explanation.body: A reporting clause can come before a quotation, interrupt it, or follow it. In literary narration, a following clause with a noun subject may allow inversion (replied the caretaker), although uninverted order is also possible. With a pronoun subject, neutral contemporary prose uses the pronoun before the reporting verb: she replied, not replied she. Use natural punctuation to show the boundary between spoken words and narrator’s text.
explanation.example: “The room is ready,” announced the caretaker. “We can begin,” she added.

explanation.heading: Negatives can negate two different things
explanation.body: To say that somebody gave no information or did not hold a thought, negate the reporting verb: he did not say where the key was. To convey a statement whose content is negative, usually put the negative inside the reported clause: he said that the key was not there. These differ logically; silence about a fact does not show that its opposite was asserted.
explanation.example: She did not say that the bridge was closed. / She said that the bridge was not closed.

explanation.heading: Negative reporting verbs with attitudes and expectations
explanation.body: With verbs of thinking, belief or expectation, English often places the negative in the reporting clause: I do not think the proposal will pass; she did not expect them to arrive. In many contexts these express an expectation of a negative outcome, but this preference is not automatic for every verb or context. Verbs such as insist and promise may require a different construction to preserve the original message.
explanation.example: I do not expect the delivery to arrive today.

explanation.heading: Questions become non-inverted subordinate clauses
explanation.body: Indirect wh-questions use a wh-word followed by ordinary statement order; yes/no questions usually use if or whether. Remove the question’s do-support unless it remains necessary for a negative verb phrase (why she did not reply). Whether, but not if, can precede a to-infinitive when reporting a decision: whether to continue. In questions like who the manager is, be and its complement can sometimes appear in either order; do not generalise this special flexibility to other verbs.
explanation.example: “Why did the alarm stop?” → They asked why the alarm had stopped. “Is it safe?” → They asked whether it was safe.

comparisons.title: Negating the report versus reporting a negative claim

left.label: Negative reporting verb
left.example: The witness did not say that the door was locked.
left.note: There is no assertion that the witness made this particular statement.

right.label: Negative reported clause
right.example: The witness said that the door was not locked.
right.note: The witness actually made a claim about the door being unlocked.

left.label: Direct question: inverted auxiliary
left.note: Did marks the direct interrogative construction.

right.label: Reported question: ordinary clause order
right.example: She asked when the parcel had arrived.
right.note: The subject precedes the verb within the indirect wh-clause.

examples.sentence: The assistant explained that the briefing would begin after lunch.
examples.note: The reporting clause identifies the speaker; the that-clause gives the content.

examples.sentence: “We have enough chairs,” observed the host.
examples.note: The noun subject can follow a reporting verb after a quotation in literary narration.
With a pronoun subject, neutral prose uses she observed rather than observed she.

examples.sentence: The caretaker did not tell us whether the heating was working.
examples.note: The reporting verb is negative: the requested information was not supplied.

examples.sentence: The inspector asked why the rear entrance had been left open.
examples.note: The embedded question begins with why and uses statement word order.

commonMistakes.why: In neutral modern narrative, a pronoun subject precedes the reporting verb.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The client asked where was the invoice.
commonMistakes.correct: The client asked where the invoice was.
commonMistakes.why: An indirect wh-question normally has statement word order.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We wondered if to postpone the rehearsal.
commonMistakes.correct: We wondered whether to postpone the rehearsal.
commonMistakes.why: Whether can introduce a to-infinitive question about a decision; if cannot.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I did not know what did the technician mean.
commonMistakes.correct: I did not know what the technician meant.
commonMistakes.why: The embedded clause does not use question-order did; tense is carried by meant.

studyTips: For each quotation, label the reporting clause separately from the speaker’s reported words before rewriting it indirectly.
Compare did not say it was unsafe with said it was not unsafe; identify which claim was or was not made.
Turn direct wh- and yes/no questions into subordinate clauses by replacing question word order with ordinary subject–verb order.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence reports a speaker’s message indirectly rather than quoting her exact words?
choices: “I have changed my mind,” Salma said.
Salma explained that she had changed her mind.
exercises.feedback: Explained that introduces a reported clause in the narrator’s wording without quotation marks.

exercises.prompt: Choose the most natural neutral reporting clause after a quotation with a pronoun subject.
choices: “The figures are correct,” he was confirm.
exercises.feedback: With a pronoun subject, he precedes the reporting verb confirmed.

exercises.prompt: Yesterday, the courier ___ explain why the package had been opened. Choose a negative reporting verb.
exercises.feedback: Did not explain negates the act of providing the information.

exercises.prompt: I could not decide ___ to accept the invitation.
exercises.feedback: Whether, unlike if, can introduce a to-infinitive expressing an unresolved decision.

exercises.prompt: Direct question: “Where does the courier leave the parcels each morning?” Report it in the present: “The receptionist asks where the courier ___ the parcels each morning.” Supply leave in the correct form.
acceptedAnswers: leaves
exercises.feedback: A reported question uses ordinary subject–verb order: the courier leaves.

exercises.prompt: Direct question: “Do we need permission to enter?” Complete: “The visitor asked ___ we needed permission to enter.” Supply either reporting conjunction.
acceptedAnswers: if
whether
exercises.feedback: Either if or whether introduces a reported yes/no question.

exercises.prompt: Direct question: “What caused the interruption?” Complete: “They asked what ___ the interruption.” Supply cause in the past simple.
acceptedAnswers: caused
exercises.feedback: What is the subject of the embedded clause, so there is no auxiliary inversion.

exercises.prompt: Direct question: “Why did you not reply?” Complete the reported question from her perspective: “She asked ___.” Use the subject I and did not.
acceptedAnswers: why I did not reply
exercises.feedback: A reported negative question retains did not but uses subject I before it.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The team asked where were the spare keys stored.
acceptedAnswers: The team asked where the spare keys were stored.
exercises.feedback: The embedded wh-clause uses statement order: subject + were stored.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The visitor wondered if to bring an umbrella.
acceptedAnswers: The visitor wondered whether to bring an umbrella.
exercises.feedback: Whether to, not if to, introduces this infinitive question.

exercises.prompt: Correct the reporting clause after the quotation: “I can explain,” insisted she.
acceptedAnswers: “I can explain,” she insisted.
exercises.feedback: In neutral usage a pronoun subject comes before insisted.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I was not sure what did the supervisor mean.
acceptedAnswers: I was not sure what the supervisor meant.
exercises.feedback: Indirect wh-clauses do not use direct-question auxiliary inversion.

speakingExercises.prompt: Direct quotation: “The estimate is provisional,” said the analyst. Report it in one past-tense sentence beginning “The analyst said that”.
acceptedAnswers: The analyst said that the estimate was provisional.
speakingExercises.feedback: A reporting clause plus that-clause conveys the original information indirectly.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the reporting clause aloud, keeping the original quotation: “It is finished,” announced she. Use neutral pronoun order.
acceptedAnswers: “It is finished,” she announced.
speakingExercises.feedback: The pronoun she precedes announced after the quotation.

speakingExercises.prompt: Negate the reporting verb, not the message. Facts: The witness / not say / the window was open. Use did not and the complete sentence.
acceptedAnswers: The witness did not say the window was open.
speakingExercises.feedback: Did not say means that no such statement was made; it does not affirm that the window was closed.

speakingExercises.prompt: Turn “Where is the departure gate?” into a reported question. Begin with “He asked” and use past tense.
acceptedAnswers: He asked where the departure gate was.
speakingExercises.feedback: The subordinate wh-clause has statement order: the departure gate was.

speakingExercises.prompt: Report the yes/no question “Is the centre open on Sundays?” Begin with “They asked” and use the past tense. Accept if or whether.
acceptedAnswers: They asked whether the centre was open on Sundays.
They asked if the centre was open on Sundays.
speakingExercises.feedback: Both whether and if introduce the reported yes/no question.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the indirect question aloud: “She wondered why was he late.”
acceptedAnswers: She wondered why he was late.
speakingExercises.feedback: Embedded questions use subject before verb, without inversion.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say one sentence using whether to: We / not know / postpone / the presentation. Use did not and the words “whether to postpone”.
acceptedAnswers: We did not know whether to postpone the presentation.
speakingExercises.feedback: Whether to introduces a question about a course of action.

speakingExercises.prompt: Give two different sentences in this order using full forms. First: no statement that it was broken. Second: a statement that it was not broken. Use “The mechanic” in both.
acceptedAnswers: The mechanic did not say it was broken. The mechanic said it was not broken.
speakingExercises.feedback: Negating say differs from reporting a negative statement.

listeningExercises.audioText: “The final decision is mine,” said the director. Later, the minutes stated that the director claimed responsibility for the decision.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which part reproduces the director’s exact words?
choices: The later summary in the minutes.
listeningExercises.feedback: The quoted sentence presents the actual words; the minutes paraphrase their content.

listeningExercises.audioText: “The workshop starts at ten,” announced the organiser. “Please arrive early,” she added.
listeningExercises.prompt: In the second quotation, who is the speaker?
listeningExercises.feedback: She refers to the organiser named in the previous reporting clause.

listeningExercises.audioText: The designer asked whether the model was ready for public display.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the five-word phrase beginning with “whether” and ending with “ready”.
acceptedAnswers: whether the model was ready
listeningExercises.feedback: The embedded yes/no question uses whether and statement word order.

listeningExercises.audioText: Aisha did not say that the network was unstable. She only said that another test was needed.
listeningExercises.feedback: The only statement attributed to Aisha concerns the need for another test.

listeningExercises.audioText: Ravi was asked whether he intended to resign. He replied that he did not intend to leave his position.
listeningExercises.prompt: What did Ravi say about his plans?
choices: He did not intend to resign.
listeningExercises.feedback: He explicitly denied any current intention to leave his position.

listeningExercises.audioText: The coordinator wondered where the guests were waiting, as no one was visible in the entrance hall.
listeningExercises.prompt: What did the coordinator want to find out?
listeningExercises.feedback: Where the guests were waiting is an indirect question about location.

listeningExercises.audioText: No one knew whether to cancel the outdoor session because the forecast kept changing.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the six-word phrase beginning with “whether” and ending with “session”.
acceptedAnswers: whether to cancel the outdoor session
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker uses whether + to-infinitive to describe an unresolved choice.

listeningExercises.audioText: The editor asked why I did not include the final paragraph in the draft.
listeningExercises.prompt: Transcribe the eight-word phrase beginning with “why” and ending with “paragraph”.
acceptedAnswers: why I did not include the final paragraph
listeningExercises.feedback: The negative embedded question retains did not and uses subject-before-auxiliary order.
